newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices rise, soybeans and lumber fall.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices rise, soybeans and lumber fall.

text.p: Coffee prices resumed their rise Monday as worries about tight supplies ignited buying by speculators.
Coffee for March delivery rose 6.25 cents to close at 145.65 cents a pound at the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, just shy of the 16-month high of 147.80 cents set on Jan. 29.
"It was all fund buying," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes, referring to professional commodity fund investors. "Stocks keep going down and the market keeps going up."
Prices have risen 40 percent since Dec. 6 on supply worries, as fresh Central American supplies usually arriving at this time of year have been delayed or hurt by weather.
A long strike at Colombia's main coffee port last month and a number of sharply lower estimates for this year's bellwether Brazilian crop have also fed buying.

Prices rose Monday after a report from the exchange of the amount of available coffee warehoused for delivery against futures contracts showed inventories fell to 543 bags to 21,051 bags as of Friday. Each bag weighs 132 pounds.

Market talk that some coffee growers in Colombia may declare a strike this week to protest a lack of debt relief from the government heightened supply jitters. But Jorge Enrique Robledo, a leader of the independent growers' group Unidad Cafetera Nacional, downplayed the possibility.

March lumber fell the $10 daily limit to $401.40 for 1,000 board feet at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange on the outlook for stepped-up Canadian shipments and reduced offers by wholesalers in cash markets.
"They are not selling for much more than they paid for the it," said Curt Cunningham of Pacific Futures Trading.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, March soybeans fell 1-1/2 cents to $7.36-3/4 a bushel after ongoing rains in Brazil's Rio Grande do Sul growing region doused sentiments about damage from heat and dryness in the Brazilian summer.
"Rain makes grain and that's why we were lower to start," said grain analyst Vic Lespinasse of Dean Witter.
Conditions remain ideal in most of Brazil's soybean growing areas and growers said it had stopped raining in Mato Grosso state, allowing the early harvest to resume.
Crop consultant Safras e Mercado in Brazil said about 8.2 million metric tons or 30 percent of the expected crop had already been sold.
March corn lost 3/4 cent to $2.69-1/2 a bushel on talk that South Korea, a big U.S. customer, bought 250,000 tons of corn from Argentina and 36,000 tons from China.

Oil prices closed mixed with forecasts for mild weather inspiring the most action and sending heating oil futures down again after Friday's sell-off. March heating oil fell 0.88 cent to 65.28 cents a gallon at the New York Mercantile Exchange.
"Heating oil is looking precarious," said Bob MacMinn, a trader and president of MPAS in Toronto.
March crude oil ended unchanged at $24.15 a barrel and March unleaded gasoline added 0.09 cent to 68.35 cents a gallon.
